decisions.statement: The script is read into the shell a bash call runs in rather than run on its own.
The file one line is appended to and that line's opening are handed in as words.
The shell joins a control group made for that one call.
That group is made under the group above, where the group above delegates processor and memory.
The group bounds the shell together with everything that shell starts.
A group this script makes is named apart from a group a run makes.
What the call spent is read as the call ends, by a trap the shell runs at exit.
A trap runs where the command exited of its own accord as well as where it ran out.
The shell leaves the group before the group is read and taken away.
A subshell reaching the trap writes nothing, since the call is the shell's own.
A shell on a machine delegating neither is weighed from its own kernel counters.
Those counters carry the seconds the shell's reaped children spent.
A call weighed that way states that its peak was not measured.
A group that would not be read leaves the call stating that its peak was not measured.
A row written before `137ed2adbee8` may say its peak was measured where nothing measured it.
The peak a group reached is the memory the call added, since a shell starts holding nothing.
Every second the call spent is a child's, since the shell is not the process recording.
Nothing here says on either stream.
Nothing here changes the status the command left.
A step that would not run leaves the call as the call was.
A command putting an exit trap of its own in place is weighed by nothing.
The group such a call left behind is swept by whoever opens the next call.

definition: what weighs one bash call from inside that call's own shell
